{{Short description|Space such that every point has a Hausdorff neighborhood}}
{{Separation axioms}}

In [[mathematics]], in the field of [[topology]], a [[topological space]] is said to be '''locally Hausdorff''' if every point has a [[neighbourhood (topology)|neighbourhood]] that is a [[Hausdorff space]] under the [[subspace topology]].<ref>{{citation|last=Niefield|first=Susan B.|title=Category theory (Como, 1990)|contribution=Weak products over a locally Hausdorff locale|publisher=Springer, Berlin|series=Lecture Notes in Math.|volume=1488|year=1991|doi=10.1007/BFb0084228|mr=1173020|pages=298–305}}.</ref>

==Examples and sufficient conditions==

* Every [[Hausdorff space]] is locally Hausdorff.
* There are locally Hausdorff spaces where a sequence has more than one limit. This can never happen for a Hausdorff space.
* The [[line with two origins]] is locally Hausdorff (it is in fact [[Locally metrizable space|locally metrizable]]) but not Hausdorff.
* The [[etale space]] for the [[Sheaf (mathematics)|sheaf]] of differentiable functions on a [[differential manifold]] is not Hausdorff, but it is locally Hausdorff.
* Let <math>X</math> be a set given the [[particular point topology]] with particular point <math>p.</math>  The space <math>X</math> is locally Hausdorff at <math>p,</math> since <math>p</math> is an [[isolated point]] in <math>X</math> and the singleton <math>\{p\}</math> is a Hausdorff neighbourhood of <math>p.</math>  For any other point <math>x,</math> any neighbourhood of it contains <math>p</math> and therefore the space is not locally Hausdorff at <math>x.</math>

==Properties==

A space is locally Hausdorff exactly if it can be written as a union of Hausdorff open subspaces.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Niefield |first1=S. B. |title=A note on the locally Hausdorff property |journal=Cahiers de topologie et géométrie différentielle |date=1983 |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=87–95 |url=http://www.numdam.org/item/?id=CTGDC_1983__24_1_87_0 |issn=2681-2398}}, Lemma 3.2</ref>  And in a locally Hausdorff space each point belongs to some Hausdorff dense open subspace.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Baillif |first1=Mathieu |last2=Gabard |first2=Alexandre |title=Manifolds: Hausdorffness versus homogeneity |journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society |date=2008 |volume=136 |issue=3 |pages=1105–1111 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-07-09100-9|doi-access=free |arxiv=math/0609098 }}, Lemma 4.2</ref>

Every locally Hausdorff space is [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub>]].{{sfn|Niefield|1983|loc=Proposition 3.4}}  The converse is not true in general.  For example, an infinite set with the [[cofinite topology]] is a [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub> space]] that is not locally Hausdorff.

Every locally Hausdorff space is [[sober space|sober]].{{sfn|Niefield|1983|loc=Proposition 3.5}}

If <math>G</math> is a [[topological group]] that is locally Hausdorff at some point <math>x \in G,</math> then <math>G</math> is Hausdorff. This follows from the fact that if <math>y \in G,</math> there exists a [[homeomorphism]] from <math>G</math> to itself carrying <math>x</math> to <math>y,</math> so <math>G</math> is locally Hausdorff at every point, and is therefore [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub>]] (and T<sub>1</sub> topological groups are Hausdorff).
